questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to learn a new language quickly
The history of the English language in modern Australia
Endangered languages, and how one came back to life
Why missionaries wrote dictionaries
questions.why: They discuss what can be done to save languages, and how Barngarla came back to life.

questions.q: What do the greetings Phil plays at the start have in common?
options: They are all from Europe
They are all very easy to learn
They all come from one family of languages
They are all endangered languages
questions.why: Phil says the one thing uniting these languages is that they're all endangered.

questions.q: What did the study by the Australian National University find?
options: Half of the world's 7,000 languages are under threat
Most languages are growing
Only 200 languages are still spoken
Australia has more languages than any other country in the world
questions.why: It found that out of the world's 7000 languages, half are under threat.

questions.q: Why did many Aboriginal languages die out?
options: People chose to speak English instead because it was useful
Children were taken away and made to learn English
There were no written dictionaries
The languages were too difficult to learn
questions.why: Neil says children were removed from their mothers and sent to schools far away to learn English.

questions.q: What is true about the Barngarla language today?
options: It has no speakers at all
Parents and children speak it, and it's taught in school
It is only used by a few older people in church services
It is only written, never spoken
questions.why: Phil says today it's spoken between parents and children, and even learned in school.

questions.q: How did Professor Ghil'ad Zuckermann help bring Barngarla back?
options: Using a dictionary written by a missionary in 1844
Recording the last native speaker
Inventing new words for it
Translating the whole Bible into Barngarla for schools
questions.why: He used a dictionary with up to 3500 words written by a German missionary in 1844.

questions.q: Why does Professor Zuckermann say “heathens” in quotation marks?
options: Because it is a Barngarla word for visitors
Because he is reading from the Bible
Because he can't remember the right word
Because he doesn't think the word is fair
questions.why: Neil says he's questioning the word and doesn't think Aboriginals are heathens at all.

questions.q: Why does Professor Zuckermann call the situation “topsy-turvy”?
options: The dictionary was printed upside down
The missionaries spoke Barngarla very badly and made mistakes
A tool once used against the language is now saving it
The language was saved by accident
questions.why: He's using a tool written for one goal to achieve the diametrically opposite goal.
